O.outcome_detail: Institutional resources and digital technology capability

cells.quote: On a systems level, Minority-Serving Institutions (MSIs), Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs), and Tribal Colleges and Universities (TCUs) are historically lower-resourced than other public and private institutions. As a result, they have stark capability deficits in new hardware, software, and digital technologies and struggle to pay for reliable broadband connections.
cells.note: Narrative report; no effect size or new comparative study design is reported.

D.treatment: Students enrolled in MSIs, HBCUs, and TCUs

O.outcome_detail: Use of learning technologies in coursework

cells.quote: Lack of resources also make it difficult for them to provide professional learning opportunities that address digital skill deficits among their faculties. It’s little wonder, therefore, that students enrolled in MSIs, HBCUs, and TCUs are less likely to use learning technologies in their course work.
cells.note: Narrative report; no effect size is printed.

O.outcome_detail: effect of mental simulation at post-test

cells.quote: One review reports a significant negative relationship between retention interval and effect of MS, indicating that the longer the time span between pre- and post-test, the weaker the effect of MS (Driskell et al., 1994).

O.outcome_detail: effect size for performance

cells.quote: One meta-analysis (Feltz et al., 1983) found results indicating that the effect of MS on cognitive tasks (M = 1.44) is significantly larger than the effect on motor (M = 0.43) or strength (M = 0.20) tasks.
cells.note: The comparison is between task types under mental simulation, not between different instructional treatments.

D.comparison: mental simulation for tasks with less cognitive involvement

O.outcome_detail: performance effectiveness

cells.quote: In one meta-analysis (Driskell et al., 1994), tasks were examined by the degree to which a task involved more or less cognitive components. The results showed that MS was more effective the more a task involved cognitive activities.
cells.note: This is a pooled association across task cognitive involvement, with no printed effect size.

O.outcome_detail: performance after mental practice

cells.quote:
It is unequivocally found that mentally practicing is more effective than engaging in no practice at all.

The consulted meta-analyses (Driskell, Copper, & Moran, 1994; Feltz et al., 1983; Hinshaw, 1991) lead to the same general conclusion that practice through MS is significantly more beneficial than no practice. Effect sizes of 0.48, 0.53 and 0.68 are reported, indicating that employment of MS influences performance positively when compared to no practice at all (Druckman, 2004; Rosnow & Rosenthal, 1996).
cells.note: The meta-review covered studies of both motor and cognitive skills and varying practice durations.

O.outcome_detail: performance on practiced skills

cells.quote: However, in some instances, sole physical practice can be more beneficial than the same time spent engaging in sole mental practice or a combination of mental practice and physical practice (Murphy, 1994; Suinn, 1997).
cells.note: The source reports this as occurring in some instances, so the direction is coded mixed rather than uniformly negative.

O.outcome_detail: performance and accuracy of mentally rehearsed motor skills

cells.quote:
It is argued that beginners at a motor task are at a larger risk of practicing a desired skill incorrectly, and thereby potentially worsening their performance instead of improving it (Hinshaw, 1991; Murphy, 1994; Suinn, 1997; Suinn, 1985).

It is also found (Guillot & Collet, 2005) that the higher the expertise level, the more accurate a movement can be mentally rehearsed in terms of temporal organization of the movement.

A higher expertise-level seems to generate performance enhancements for both cognitive and motor skills.
cells.note: The entry's quoted claim concerns the risk of incorrect rehearsal among beginners and the greater rehearsal accuracy associated with expertise; the synthesis does not provide a single printed comparative effect size.
